title: Ice-dynamic regime of the Northeast Greenland Ice Stream derived from the mass flux balance of englacial units
abstract: An assumption commonly used for ice streams in ice sheet models is that the vertical profile of horizontal velocity is constant throughout the ice column from the surface to the base.Here, we use airborne radar data for mass flux balance analysis of the central part of the Northeast Greenland Ice Stream, to ascertain whether this assumption is broadly applicable in the ice stream's central region where the ice flow appears to be channelled by a large subglacial trough.We investigate the along-flow evolution of mass flux balance of both the full ice thickness and three englacial units in steady-state, and analyse the spatial variation of their imbalances.We assess the potential over-and under-estimation of ice flow velocity within the ice column and infer vertical shear profile models for our study region.These inferences suggest that the ice stream in this central region is flowing as a block, or plugflow, rather than with deformation from internal shearing, despite large variations in bed topography, basal shear stresses, and in a region with relatively slow ice flow velocities.

title: Permafrost carbon–climate feedback amplifies Earth system tipping risks
abstract: Abstract Global warming leads to widespread permafrost thaw and subsequent emissions of carbon dioxide and methane, driving the permafrost carbon–climate feedback (PCF) which amplifies climate change. Many current-generation climate models omit this feedback, limiting projections of long-term temperature outcomes and associated Earth system tipping risks. Here, we investigate how this feedback affects the risk and timing of crossing tipping points in the Earth system by integrating permafrost carbon emissions into temperature projections for idealized stabilization and overshoot scenarios. In a conceptual network model of interacting climate tipping elements—including the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, and the Amazon rainforest, we find that PCF leads to additional warming that increases the probability of exceeding one or more tipping elements by up to 50% and can substantially accelerate the timing of tipping events by hundreds of years. The effect of PCF on tipping risk and acceleration is particularly evident in overshoot scenarios with lower peak temperatures below 2–3 ∘ C or peak cumulative emissions of below 2000 PgC. Considering PCF, therefore, narrows the critical temperature space for overshoot pathways. Our results highlight that failing to account for PCF underestimates both climate risks and the urgency of mitigation, increasing the likelihood of tipping events across the Earth system.

title: Solid-Earth geophysics and geodesy in Antarctica: achievements, current capabilities, and future directions
abstract: The Antarctic Ice Sheet (AIS) plays a major role in the global climate, providing a natural laboratory to study the processes that interlink the cryosphere, solid Earth, atmosphere, and hydrosphere. Through its ongoing mass loss, the AIS currently contributes to global-mean sea-level rise at a rate of 0.4 mm a −1 . However, its impact on and feedback with climate and sea-level changes are still poorly understood. To generate reliable sea-level projections for the future, there is an urgent need to substantially improve our knowledge of the solid-Earth properties and subsequent response to ice-mass variations in space and time. This issue has been identified as a key question by the international community, strongly supported by the Scientific Committee on Antarctic Research (SCAR). We review how state-of-the-art Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) and seismic networks in Antarctica, in combination with further ground-based, airborne and satellite-based geophysical measurements, have been used to significantly advance our understanding of solid-Earth processes and their impact on the cryosphere. Future research activities should be coordinated to answer the most urgent science questions. For example, how can we consistently test and model, respectively, a realistic mantle rheology that includes lateral inhomogeneity and transient relaxation, together with AIS mass changes on all time scales since the Last Glacial Maximum, including Holocene retreat and readvance? What processes and boundary conditions should coupled ice-sheet/gravity-rotation-deformation models include in order to realistically reflect the complex interaction between the solid Earth, ice sheet and ocean? Based on the recent achievements and the most urgent science questions, a vision is articulated for science-driven, multidisciplinary geophysical observations and corresponding technological developments. Long-term observations and improved modelling must be combined to develop precise and reliable projections for Antarctica's future mass change and associated contribution to sea-level change at both regional and global scales.

title: Ice surface change drives subglacial hydrologic reorganization and interior speedup in northwest Greenland
abstract: Abstract Changes in ice surface elevation and slope influence subglacial water pressure and sliding velocity. Leveraging changes in elevation observed by the Ice, Cloud and land-Elevation satellite (ICESat) and ICESat-2 missions, we use coupled subglacial hydrology–ice dynamics modeling applied to a section of the northwest Greenland ice sheet to explore (i) how decadal-scale changes in ice surface elevation influence changes in winter background subglacial hydrology and corresponding ice velocity, and (ii) how much seasonal response is attributable to geometry versus environmental forcing. Our simulations suggest complex reorganization of the subglacial hydrologic system between 2004 and 2020, resulting from changes in surface elevation, driving redistribution of freshwater flux, an overall acceleration trend in the interior and an increase in background basal melt. Without changing hydrological conditions, geometry changes alone lead to greater interior acceleration, suggesting that changes in the subglacial system help to mitigate this speedup. We also find that the winter background state of the subglacial system modulates the seasonal response. This work demonstrates feedbacks that influence mass loss from the Greenland ice sheet as surface elevation evolves, highlighting the subtleties involved in accounting for changes in effective pressure, ice velocity and basal melt due to changes in subglacial hydrology.

title: Sea ice variability and links to East Siberian permafrost carbon remobilization during the last glacial-interglacial transition
abstract: Sea ice is an important regulator of the Arctic climate systems. Records of sea ice past instrumental records are necessary to understand how sea ice is altered during past periods of abrupt climate change, and what consequences such changes have on the polar climates. Here, we reconstructed the sea ice cover of the East Siberian Arctic and found that the sea ice extent likely was linked to protecting/eroding permafrost coastlines during the last deglaciation.

title: The balance of evidence indicates a slowing AMOC
abstract: arXiv:2611.23429v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a critical component of the climate system. Climate models have long predicted a slowing of the AMOC due to anthropogenic forcing, with a risk of passing tipping points in the future. The question of whether the AMOC is already weakening is still somewhat controversial. Continuous monitoring is only available for the past two decades, a period too short to tease apart contributions of natural variability and climate change. Reconstructions of AMOC strength going back further in time have different limitations which are debated in the literature. Here we compile and discuss this heterogeneous body of evidence, focusing on latitudes south of 45{\deg}N where northward and southward flow are separated vertically. We conclude that the balance of multiple lines of evidence strongly supports a past and ongoing AMOC slowing in response to global warming, although some uncertainty remains regarding its magnitude and timing.

title: Twenty Years of data from the RAPID-MOCHA-WBTS array: Long-Term Changes in the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, Heat and Freshwater Transports
abstract: Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) For over 20 years, measurements across the Atlantic at 26° N has continuously recorded the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation that carry heat northward and help shape the climate. This paper describes the resulting data, how they are produced and shared, and how they show changes in these ocean circulation over time. It also releases the computer code used to produce them, so anyone can reproduce and reuse the data.

title: Intra-annual grounding-line migration and retreat: insights from high-resolution satellite and in situ observations over Milne Glacier in the Canadian High Arctic
abstract: Arctic glaciers that flow into the ocean are changing rapidly due to climate warming. The grounding line, where these glaciers transition from land to ocean, is critical to their stability. We examined Milne Glacier in the Canadian High Arctic using satellite, field, and modelled data. Our study shows how changes in ice flow and ice bending near the grounding line affect satellite-based mapping of this area and documents a newly discovered grounding-line retreat associated with subglacial ridges.

title: Landscape evolution at an emerging englacial esker in Southeast Iceland over weekly-to-annual timescales
abstract: Abstract Eskers are used to characterize glacial drainage systems to inform ice-sheet modeling. However, the connection between eskers preserved in the paleoglaciologic record and the conditions required to deposit them is not well understood, particularly for englacial eskers. We use uncrewed aerial vehicle data over weekly-to-annual timescales from 2021 to 2024 at Breiðamerkurjökull in Iceland to investigate how englacial eskers evolve after emerging from the glacier. During the study period, an esker emerged from an englacial conduit, experienced significant modification and was emplaced on the outwash plain at the edge of a proglacial lake. We find that englacial eskers experience significant erosion and modification as they interact with proglacial lakes or streams and their ice cores melt, implying that englacial eskers are not generally well preserved in the paleoglaciologic record. Both esker morphology and stratigraphy evolved over the study period, indicating that when observed in preserved englacial eskers, they do not necessarily reflect conduit emplacement conditions. Englacial eskers deposited at the edge of overdeepenings may be more likely to be preserved than those deposited elsewhere. Additionally, surface ice topography evolution is assessed to identify structural hazards at an esker-forming glacier margin, which is critical as glacial-related hazards increase in a warming climate.

title: Research progress on the geomorphic evolution of the Taihu Lake Basin since the LGM and its implications for the human living environment
abstract: The coupling between Neolithic cultural vicissitudes and paleogeomorphic evolution is a core issue in environmental archaeological research in the lower reaches of the Yangtze River. Based on a synthesis and analysis of advances in environmental archaeology over the past few decades, the study systematically reviews and evaluates key scientific issues such as sea-level changes in eastern China since the Last Glacial Maximum, the geomorphic evolution processes in the Taihu Lake Basin, and their impacts on the distribution of Neolithic sites, with a focus on discussing controversial issues such as the existence of the Holocene high sea-level stand, the genesis of the “present-day Taihu Lake”, and the causes of the collapse of the Liangzhu culture. In addition, by synthesizing the prehistoric subsistence strategies, the study offers new insights into the prospection of Neolithic sites predating 7 ka BP. The results demonstrate that the sea-level in East China commenced a period of rapid rise following the end of the LGM. The rate of rise then decreased at ∼7 ka BP, shifting to a slower rise phase with subsequent fluctuating upward trends. A mid-Holocene high sea-level stand occurred during ∼7–4 ka BP, with sea-level ∼2 m higher than present-day level. Furthermore, the geomorphic evolution of the Taihu Lake Basin stems from the long-term superimposition and coupling of multiple driving factors. It underwent successive stages of “paleosurface formation”, “hummocky terrace formation”, “chenier ridge formation”, and “dish-shaped depression formation”. During ∼7–3 ka BP, the area experienced a geomorphic reversal stage, evolving from a hummocky terrace toward a lake-plain landscape centered on dish-shaped depressions. The spatial distribution of Neolithic sites in this region closely responds to geomorphic and environmental changes, revealing a distinct human migration pattern: settlements shifted from uplands to plains and subsequently to high coastal areas. The collapse of the Liangzhu culture was primarily triggered by frequent flooding events, which were jointly induced by ENSO-enhanced precipitation variability and sea-level rise under cold and dry climatic conditions. Neolithic sites predating 7 ka BP may be preserved on elevated terraces and paleochannel terraces formed during the terminal LGM.

title: Characterizing ENSO Teleconnections Impact on Gross Primary Productivity across CMIP6 Earth System Models
abstract: Abstract The El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is the dominant mode of interannual variability in the climate system, altering global circulation patterns and causing changes in temperature and precipitation in remote regions through teleconnections. Because ecosystems are sensitive to climate variations, ENSO teleconnections have large implications for the magnitude of carbon uptake by terrestrial vegetation at interannual timescales. Using ten CMIP6 Earth System Models during 1950–2014, we find global carbon uptake is reduced 0.68± 0.18 PgC per °C increase in the Nino3.4 sea surface temperature, primarily due to reduced gross primary productivity (GPP), with a secondary contribution from increased heterotrophic respiration. We quantify the ENSO impact on GPP and identify several key regions in the tropics (Amazon, Southeast Asia) and extratropics (Australia, Northwest North America) where the ensemble shows regionally coherent, statistically significant changes to GPP. In the Amazon, most models suppress GPP due to increased temperature, but three models exhibit a weaker reduction or slight enhancement in GPP. Inter-model differences in background soil moisture state mediate the relative importance of temperature compared to radiation in controlling total and ENSO-driven GPP variability in the Amazon, with drier models exhibiting a stronger temperature-driven response and tending to exhibit greater reductions in GPP associated with ENSO. Our results suggest that, across the ensemble, land model sensitivities to simulated physical climate anomalies play a large role in the GPP response to ENSO conditions and that these responses differ regionally even within the same latitude range.

title: A multi-decadal dataset of surface damage  on Antarctic ice shelves (1999–2024)
abstract: Many Antarctic ice shelves are thinning and retreating, threatening future sea-level rise. Surface damage indicates structural weakening, but long-term records are scarce. We created a multi-decadal surface damage record for nine representative Antarctic ice shelves using satellite imagery and deep learning. Among them, Pine Island, Thwaites and Scar Inlet have experienced the most significant changes in surface damage during the study period, providing insights into ice shelf stability.

title: Proglacial lakes substantially modulate the surface mass balance of deglacial ice sheets
abstract: Towards the end of the last ice age large proglacial lakes formed at the margins of the retreating ice sheets, potentially staying cold due to the influence of melting ice. Modeling shows these lakes lowered summer air temperatures, increased snowfall, and in total reduced surface melt by 18 %–27 % for nearby ice sheets. If lakes stayed below 4 °C, melt dropped by 23 %–35 %, providing a substantial negative feedback for retreating of ice sheets.

title: Long‐Term Surface Meltwater Variability and Surface Fracture Patterns on the Amery Ice Shelf
journal: New Zealand Journal of Geology and Geophysics
abstract: Antarctic ice shelves buttress grounded ice, but surface meltwater can promote fracture opening when it enters pre‐existing crevasses. Although meltwater variability, water depth and fracture features have been examined separately on the Amery Ice Shelf, their spatial correspondence has received less attention. We integrated January meltwater maps for 2005–2026 with depth and volume estimates for melt seasons ending in 2014–2026 within a common spatial framework. Fracture inputs comprised published creavasse extraction maps for 2009 and 2014 and a Landsat‐derived map for 2025. Multi‐year melt water and creavess coupling indices described relative spatial co‐location. Seasonal indices combined water proximity, local fracture context and retrieved depth. Estimated seasonal volume peaked at 0.76 km 3 in 2017 and 0.75 km 3 in 2019. The 2025 volume was 0.44 km 3 , with generally smaller retrieved depths than in 2014 and 2017. January mapped meltwater area ranged from 26.2 km 2 in 2021 to 1178.1 km 2 in 2005 and reached 1058.4 km 2 in 2025. Recurrently mapped meltwater was concentrated in western and southwestern sectors and along central flow‐aligned zones. The fracture maps showed broadly similar regional zones. The 2014 and 2025 seasonal indices had higher relative values in the western and southwestern sectors. The multi‐year recurrence–fracture comparison showed a similar regional concentration. Adding maximum retrieved depth from seasons ending in 2014–2025 further localised the highest relative multi‐year index values in these sectors. The southeastern sector contained extensive mapped fractures with comparatively limited hydrological co‐location. These results identify regional concentrations of recurrently mapped meltwater, greater retrieved depth and mapped fractures.

title: Expansion of North Atlantic Deep Water during Northern Hemisphere Glaciation
abstract: Abstract Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a major driver of the Earth’s climate, moving heat from the Southern Hemisphere to the Northern Hemisphere. Neither foraminiferal carbon isotope records nor modelling studies agree on the spatial extent of North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW), the northern deep limb of the AMOC, over the intensification of Northern Hemisphere Glaciation (iNHG, ~2.73 million years ago). Here we present high-resolution neodymium isotope (ε Nd ) records from a depth transect in the equatorial Atlantic over the iNHG. We find a persistent latitudinal and depth gradient in neodymium isotope values in the deep Atlantic during the Late Pliocene, absent in the Early Pleistocene, indicating an expansion of NADW extent over the iNHG. In contrast, our reconstruction suggests very little glacial-interglacial variability in NADW extent during both the Late Pliocene and Early Pleistocene. These results suggest deep-water circulation was substantially different during a warm climate state, with implications for the role of NADW formation during major climate transitions and its future stability.

title: Evidence for subglacial flooding in labyrinthine channels on Devon Island, Nunavut, Canada
abstract: We describe the morphological characteristics of anastomosing (labyrinthine) bedrock channels to enhance the current understanding of subglacial meltwater dynamics of the Innuitian Ice Sheet. Our work reveals a morphological similarity between labyrinthine channels and other landscapes modified by glacial floods. We argue that the presence of anastomosis, distinct erosional surfaces, and longitudinal profile slope breaks imply formation by short-lived episodes of erosion associated with floods.

title: Isotope-based age scale with multi-month precision for the SE-Dome II ice core from Southeast Greenland over the past 150 years
abstract: We developed a new 150-year age scale for an ice core from southeast Greenland by matching its oxygen-isotope variations with climate-model simulations. The record resolves changes over several months and shows that snowfall remained nearly evenly distributed through the seasons from 1871 to 2020. This stability suggests that the regional balance of atmospheric circulation and moisture transport changed little at this site despite recent Arctic warming.

title: Sub-daily multi-pass AMSR2 passive microwave response to the 2012 extreme melt event in northwestern Greenland
abstract: The unprecedented Greenland Ice Sheet melt in summer 2012 provides a natural experiment to evaluate how spaceborne passive microwave brightness temperature ( T B ) responds to extreme melt on diurnal timescales. We analyzed multi-frequency AMSR2 T B from GCOM–W over a northwestern Greenland site (SIGMA–A) and compared the radiometric evolution with in situ snow temperatures and surface energy balance terms derived from automated weather station meteorology. From early to mid-July 2012, T B showed coherent, frequency- and polarization-dependent transitions through the major melt event, including a pronounced shift in diurnal behavior. Outside the melt peak, high-frequency T B (36.5 and 89.0 GHz) exhibited clear day–night contrast, whereas during the extreme melt period T B remained elevated with a strongly damped diurnal range, consistent with sustained nighttime wetness. At 89.0 GHz, T B increases coincided with persistently positive surface energy input dominated by enhanced downward longwave radiation and peak cloud occurrence inferred from Aqua/MODIS and all-sky imagery, supporting a cloud-linked high-frequency enhancement. In contrast, low-frequency T B (6.9–10.7 GHz) decreased, most strongly in H-pol, consistent with melt-driven reductions in effective emissivity associated with wet–dry dielectric contrasts. Most notably, the 6.9–7.3 GHz difference revealed a distinct polarization-dependent post-melt transition: after the melt peak, Δ T B, H showed increased variability and occasional positive values, whereas Δ T B, V remained nearly unchanged at negative values. This behavior indicates that the 6.9–7.3 GHz H-pol pair is sensitive not only to melt-driven changes in low-frequency emission, but also to refreezing-modified near-surface stratigraphy. These results demonstrate that multi-frequency microwave radiometry can resolve rapid snow–firn transitions during extreme melt and identify the 6.9–7.3 GHz H-pol difference as a compact diagnostic that complements conventional melt monitoring by capturing post-melt near-surface structural evolution.

title: Early warning of critical transitions: Distinguishing tipping points from turing destabilizations
abstract: Current early warning signs for tipping points often fail to distinguish between catastrophic shifts and less dramatic state changes, such as spatial pattern formation. This paper introduces a novel method that addresses this limitation by providing more information about the type of bifurcation being approached starting from a spatially homogeneous system state. This method relies on estimates of the dispersion relation from noisy spatio-temporal data, which reveals whether the system is approaching a spatially homogeneous (tipping) or spatially heterogeneous (Turing patterning) bifurcation. Using a modified Klausmeier model, we validate this method on synthetic data, exploring its performance under varying conditions including noise properties and distance to bifurcation. We also determine the data requirements for optimal performance. Our results indicate the promise of a new spatial early warning system built on this method to improve predictions of future transitions in many climate subsystems and ecosystems, which is critical for effective conservation and management in a rapidly changing world.

title: The cryosphere beyond a planetary safe operating space
abstract: The cryosphere plays a vital role in regulating planetary dynamics and habitability, yet it remains unclear whether its essential functions remain within a safe operating space (SOS) amid Anthropocene change. Here, we propose a cryosphere SOS and systematically evaluate its contributions to Earth system resilience using the planetary boundaries framework. Multiple lines of evidence indicate an accelerating and partly irreversible loss of cryospheric integrity, driven by amplifying feedbacks. Key cryospheric control variables either have left or are committed to departing from Holocene-like conditions. We conclude that the cryosphere has breached its SOS and is on a trajectory that locks in long-term risks for human societies and ecosystems. Safeguarding planetary resilience therefore requires explicit consideration of cryosphere change and its interactions across the Earth system.

Oxygen isotopes reveal a significant Middle Pleistocene transition from temperate rainforest to arid desert-like conditions in eastern Australia
abstract: Reconstructing terrestrial palaeoenvironmental change during the Middle Pleistocene is essential for understanding ecosystem stability and resilience under long-term climatic forcing. However, well-dated, quantitative records from Australia remain limited. Fossil deposits at Mount Etna Caves, central eastern Queensland, preserve two taxonomically distinct faunal assemblages that have been interpreted as a substantial ecological transition from a diverse rainforest system to an arid-adapted faunal community. Previous interpretations of this transition have relied primarily on faunal evidence, with limited site-specific geochemical validation. Here, we integrate oxygen isotope (δ 18 O) analyses of fossil macropodid enamel with refined in-situ U-Th geochronology to reconstruct changes in hydroclimatic conditions across this transition. New U-Th ages better constrain deposition of the arid-adapted assemblage to a narrow interval between 199 ± 5 and 205 ± 4 ka. Fossils from older deposits (pre-280 ka) exhibit consistently low δ 18 O values (−2.59 ± 0.54 ‰), suggesting relatively humid conditions, whereas the younger deposit is markedly enriched (4.59 ± 1.92 ‰). Random Forest classification models trained on modern macropodine δ 18 O data suggest that pre-280 ka assemblages show strongest similarity with humid temperate forest environments analogous to modern temperate oceanic (Cfb-like) systems of southeastern Australia and highland New Guinea. In contrast, the post-205 ka assemblages show the strongest affinity with arid, hot desert (BWh-like) conditions characteristic of central Australia. This transition coincides with broader Middle Pleistocene climatic reorganisation centred on ∼270 ka, which may have contributed to sustained regional drying. These findings suggest that long-term climatic forcing may push ecosystems beyond hydroclimatic thresholds, resulting in major ecological reorganisation, altered species distributions, and reduced biogeographic connectivity. By providing a directly dated, multi-proxy terrestrial record, this study highlights how substantial environmental change during the Quaternary offers an important analogue for understanding ecosystem vulnerability under ongoing and future climate change.

title: Development of a semi-persistent floating terminus at San Quintín Glacier (Northern Patagonia Icefield), the last piedmont glacier in the Andes
abstract: Abstract The piedmont lobe of San Quintín Glacier, the largest outlet of the Northern Patagonia Icefield, has recently entered a phase of rapid frontal retreat. We present results from a helicopter-borne ground-penetrating radar (GPR) survey conducted in May 2019 in the terminal zone of the glacier, combined with satellite-derived ice velocity, frontal position and surface elevation change data. GPR measurements along the flowline indicate ice thicknesses of 215–240 m in the lowermost 1400 m of the glacier. The inferred grounding line is located approximately 1500 m upstream from the 2019 calving front. Analysis of surface elevation change in 2017–19 shows mean thinning rates of -5.43 plus or minus $\pm$ ± 1.58 m a minus 1 $^{-1}$ − 1 upstream and -1.08 plus or minus $\pm$ ± 1.39 m a minus 1 $^{-1}$ − 1 near the terminus. Satellite-derived velocities reach up to 1050 m a minus 1 $^{-1}$ − 1 in the lower glacier, with higher values observed in the later part of the observation period. Residual bed reflection power derived from the GPR profiles indicates the presence of water at the glacier bed in the terminal zone. Taken together, these observations are consistent with the development of a semi-persistent floating terminus, where basal water and buoyancy modulate surface elevation change and control frontal stability and calving style. The results provide new observational constraints on the transient behaviour of floating termini at fast-flowing outlet glaciers in lacustrine settings.

title: Coupled Ocean–Atmosphere Processes Associated with Realistically Sized Weddell Sea Polynyas in CMIP6 Models
abstract: Abstract The mechanisms of the Weddell Sea Polynya have been frequently discussed in the literature since the first and largest observed opening in the 1970s, with smaller Maud Rise Polynyas opening in more recent years. Here we assess both the oceanic and atmospheric preconditioning and response associated with polynya events, using Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) Pre-industrial Control models. Here, we focus on polynyas with realistic size and location (i.e., comparable to the 1970s events). Only two models in the CMIP6 suite produce such realistic polynyas in large numbers, ACCESS-ESM1.5 and MPI-ESM1-2-HR. Their oceanic and atmospheric preconditioning and atmospheric response are explored using a composite analysis. We find that weakened stratification sets the oceanic preconditioning, while the onset of polynya years is associated with the occurrence of large-scale atmospheric internal variability, including a ZW3-like pressure and wind pattern. Both modes emerge from internal atmospheric variability, suggesting that the first occurrence in a series of polynya years is stochastic in nature. Once the polynya opens, two-way air-sea feedbacks deepen the sea level pressure anomalies, enabling multi-year polynya events. Through this, the stratification returns to a base level, the ocean state recharges, and the cycle repeats. These results advance understanding of Weddell Sea Polynya formation and highlight the importance of coupled ocean–atmosphere feedbacks in the Southern Ocean.

title: High-Resolution Cyclostratigraphy Uncovers Variable Orbital Forcing in the Oligocene South China Sea
abstract: The Oligocene provides an important interval for examining climatic and sedimentary variability following the Eocene–Oligocene transition, but the expression of orbital forcing in low-latitude marginal seas remains incompletely understood. We integrate natural gamma-ray (GR) logging and microfossil records from Well L9 in the Pearl River Mouth Basin, northern South China Sea, to establish a cyclostratigraphic framework spanning approximately 34.6–21.7 Ma. A floating chronology based on 405 kyr cycle counting was anchored using an independently constrained Oligocene–Miocene boundary horizon. Spectral analyses identify approximately 405 kyr, 100 kyr, and 40 kyr components, together with longer-period variability near 2.4 Myr and 1.2 Myr. Amplitude-modulation analysis reveals an approximately 1.2 Myr component in the 40 kyr envelope, supporting an obliquity-related interpretation. In contrast, the 100 kyr envelope contains approximately 1.6 Myr variability rather than a clear 2.4 Myr component, leaving the eccentricity-modulation origin of the latter unresolved. Palynological evidence indicates generally cool and humid conditions during the early–middle Oligocene, followed by late Oligocene warming. Comparison with published climate records suggests correspondence with six recognized cooling episodes, although chronological uncertainty limits precise event alignment. These results provide a regional chronological and paleoenvironmental framework and highlight the need to distinguish observed long-period sedimentary variability from its proposed orbital origin.

title: Using a Gaussian process emulator to approximate short-term climate response patterns to greenhouse gas and aerosol forcings
abstract: We present a fast machine learning emulator that predicts how Earth's surface temperature reacts within the first five years to changes in greenhouse gases and aerosol pollutants. It is trained on carefully designed simulations from a complex climate model, but can be run much faster. Our emulator can be used to show where the climate is most sensitive to different emissions and can help explore many possible future paths, making it easier to assess the climate effects of policy choices.

title: An antiplane shear model for evaluating shear-margin stability (Ortholine v1.0)
abstract: The widths of glaciers and ice streams can change over time, which strongly affects how much ice is lost to the ocean. Many existing models of sea-level rise neglect these width changes, but they are commonly observed and important. This paper presents a new, simple model that helps identify which physical factors govern width changes at different field sites. The model is explained step by step and tested using an Antarctic ice stream as an example.

title: Post-depositional geochemical transformations of aerosol impurities in EPICA Dome C ice core: dissolution, mineral neoformation, and immobilization revealed by CFA-sp-ICP-TOFMS
abstract: Deep ice cores preserve records of past climate, but chemical reactions inside the ice can blur these signals over time. To find out how, we studied millions of dust particles in a deep Antarctic ice core. We found that, over long timescales, dust dissolves and reforms into new minerals within tiny pockets of liquid, trapping chemical elements. Warm temperatures speed up this process. Accounting for it helps scientists interpret ancient climate records from deep ice more reliably.

title: Extreme glacier melt on the Central Tibetan Plateau during the summer of 2022: detection and mechanisms
abstract: Extreme glacier melt events accelerate mass loss, increase glacier instability, and temporarily increase downstream runoff, potentially alleviating drought conditions. Yet the glacier energy–mass balance in the Geladandong region – a headwater region of the Yangtze River (China's longest river) and one of the source regions feeding Siling Co (Tibet's largest lake) – and its connection to the unprecedented 2022 summer melt remain insufficiently quantified. To address this gap, we integrated in-situ mass balance observations and glacio-meteorological data from a 5700 m monitoring site with an energy-mass balance model and applied a novel dual-threshold framework (based on mean and standard deviation) to identify extreme mass loss/melt events in short-term glacier mass balance records. Our novel methodology identified 2021/22 as a period of extreme mass loss and melt intensity, with melt during the 2022 summer heatwave reaching unprecedented extremes. These heatwaves caused an increase in melt amount of 317.8 mm w.e., amounting to 1.66 and 1.69 times the values recorded for the same period in 2019/20 and 2020/21, respectively. This extreme melt was driven by energy balance anomalies over the glacier surface. In terms of net contributions to the +28.2 W m −2 melt energy anomaly during the three identified heatwave windows, enhanced sensible heat flux was the largest term (+17.0 W m −2 ; 60.3 %), followed by increased net longwave radiation (+14.0 W m −2 ; 49.7 %) and increased net shortwave radiation (+5.1 W m −2 ; 18.1 %) associated with reduced albedo, with negative contributions from latent heat flux and subsurface heat flux. Such anomalies were driven by large-scale atmospheric circulation patterns, specifically the eastward extension and northward displacement of the South Asian High (SAH), together with near-neutral mid-latitude westerlies. This study advances the understanding of glacier mass balance responses to extreme weather and climate events on the central Tibetan Plateau.

title: DDA-BNN v1.0: a morphology-aware surrogate model for  the optical properties of black carbon-containing particles
abstract: We developed a surrogate model to predict how black carbon particles absorb and scatter light based on their size, shape, and mixing with other aerosol species. The model was trained on detailed physics simulations and also estimates uncertainty caused by limited training data and unresolved internal structures. It outperformed common simplified particle assumptions, especially for scattering, and can help target new simulations to improve predictions of black carbon's radiative effects.

title: Divergent Evolution Patterns of Glacier Meltwater and Implications for Downstream Water Utilization in Inland River Basins of the Northern Tibetan Plateau During 1976–2024
abstract: The controls on glacier meltwater change and their implications for water supply risks remain unclear in glacier-fed inland river basins. We reconstructed glacier meltwater changes during 1976–2024 in eight representative basins of the northern Tibetan Plateau using a degree-day factor model and assessed its contribution to mountain-outlet runoff and downstream water use. Independent evaluation using the 2018 glacier inventory showed relative errors of 0.34–9.85% across the eight basins. Glacier storage decreased in all basins after the basin-specific segmentation years, while meltwater increased in most basins but declined in the Yarkand River Basin. These contrasting responses highlight substantial spatial differences in glacier meltwater evolution despite widespread glacier storage loss and increasing summer temperatures. The multi-year mean contribution of glacier meltwater to mountain-outlet runoff ranged from 1.2% to 54.3% across the eight basins, with declining contributions after the segmentation years in several highly glacierized basins. In the Hexi Corridor, annual glacier meltwater in the Shule River Basin was equivalent to about 20–40% of downstream water use. Glacier meltwater contributions to low-flow runoff increased in the three Hexi Corridor basins and in the Golmud and Buha River basins, but decreased in the Yarkand and Hotan River basins. These findings suggest potential implications of glacier storage loss for low-flow support and seasonal water supply risks, particularly in basins with substantial downstream irrigation and ecological water demands.

title: Enabling joint chemical and meteorological data assimilation with an atmospheric foundation model
abstract: arXiv:2611.24020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The hydroxyl radical (OH) is the main oxidant in the troposphere and accounts for 88% of the methane sink, yet its abundance and trends remain poorly constrained. Satellites observe many of the chemical and meteorological drivers of OH, but assimilating both requires a model that represents chemistry and meteorology together. Existing chemistry-climate models are too expensive for joint data assimilation. Here, we present AuroraChem, a fine-tuned version of the Aurora atmospheric foundation model that jointly simulates meteorology and the GEOS-Chem chemical fields needed to constrain OH. A one-year AuroraChem rollout takes 12 minutes on one GPU. Free rollouts remain stable for one year but do not fully capture seasonal cycles. Using idealized data assimilation, we find that chemical observations can constrain the meteorological state and meteorological observations can constrain the chemical state. Inserting only the chemical fields raises the annual mean spatial correlation of 500 hPa temperature from 0.89 to 0.92 and recovers the moisture and circulation pattern of the Indian summer monsoon. Inserting only the meteorological fields raises the 500 hPa OH correlation from 0.89 to 0.93, close to the 0.94 from inserting the chemical fields themselves, and recovers the OH seasonal cycle. Inserting only NO2 columns sampled at TROPOMI pixels gives an OH correlation of 0.93. These relationships likely reflect learned covariances rather than physical coupling, and covariances are what data assimilation uses to let an observation of one variable update the others. AuroraChem therefore provides a new pathway to joint chemical and meteorological data assimilation.

title: MAIC-2 v2.3: A Fortran program for simulating the surface temperature, atmospheric water transport and surface glaciation of the planet Mars
abstract: arXiv:2611.23643v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Mars Atmosphere-Ice Coupler MAIC-2 is a computationally efficient, zonally-averaged model designed to simulate Martian surface temperature, atmospheric water transport and surface glaciation over timescales of 10^5 to 10^7 years. While sophisticated General Circulation Models (GCMs) provide high-resolution simulations of the Martian atmosphere, their high computational cost makes them largely unsuitable for studies covering millions of years of orbital evolution. MAIC-2 addresses this gap by utilizing physically-based, zonally-averaged parameterizations, including a Local Insolation Temperature (LIT) scheme and a mass balance engine driven by free-convection and instantaneous mixing physics. Version 2.3 introduces a fully modularized Fortran architecture that improves maintainability and ensures that the software remains entirely self-contained, requiring no external numerical libraries or specialized data formats for execution. Demonstrated through a 20-million-year transient simulation, the model successfully reproduces the primary characteristics of the Martian polar layered deposits. MAIC-2 provides the planetary science community with a versatile, open-source tool for investigating the long-term climatic impacts of orbital variations on the Martian surface.

title: Global Holocene Stalagmite Growth Rates and Their Climatic Associations
abstract: Stalagmite growth rates record cave carbonate deposition and environmental change, but their climatic associations remain insufficiently tested at the global Holocene scale. We compiled 218 stalagmites from 139 caves in SISALv3, calculated mean Holocene growth rates, and matched their growth intervals to gridded paleoclimate variables. Spearman rank correlations, partial least-squares regression, and XGBoost classification were used to assess climatic associations. Growth rates ranged from 0.003 to 1.75 mm yr−1, with 75% of samples below 0.1248 mm yr−1. Annual precipitation showed a weak positive correlation with growth rate (ρ = 0.161), whereas wettest-quarter precipitation, precipitation seasonality, precipitation concentration, and wet-season precipitation ratio showed stronger correlations with growth rate (ρ = 0.288–0.306). Temperature associations were more consistent: mean annual, coldest-quarter, and wettest-quarter temperatures were positively correlated with growth rate (ρ = 0.356–0.422), while temperature seasonality was negatively correlated (ρ = −0.328). An XGBoost model using five climate variables achieved 69.32% accuracy in two-fold cross-validation. These results indicate that climate captures part of the spatial variability in stalagmite growth. Growth rates reflect the combined effects of effective recharge, thermal conditions, karst hydrology, and cave depositional environments, providing a global reference for interpreting Holocene stalagmite records.

title: Short-Campaign GNSS Observations of Horizontal Velocity and Vertical Tidal Response Across the Drygalski Ice Tongue, East Antarctica
abstract: The Drygalski Ice Tongue is a tide-influenced floating extension of the David Glacier in East Antarctica, where field observations are constrained by polar logistics. We investigated how horizontal ice motion and vertical tidal response vary along and across the tongue. To extend earlier observations, we analysed a 2025–2026 Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) campaign comprising 12 stations and 248 station-days. Kinematic GNSS coordinate series were produced with Bernese 5.4 and subsequently analysed under four stochastic covariance descriptions for horizontal and apparent vertical-rate estimation. Comparisons with a regional Mario Zucchelli Station (MZS)/Terra Nova Bay tide reference characterized station-level up-component response to tidal forcing, and two tide-removal paths were evaluated for apparent vertical-rate analysis. Floating-tongue speeds increased downstream, spanning 663.9–749.4 m/yr, with a clockwise turn toward the southeast and north-to-south differences in fitted campaign rates. The main horizontal patterns persisted across all four tested covariance descriptions. Vertical tidal response was weak in the near-grounding group, spatially heterogeneous in the transition sector, and near-unity downstream. Across the four covariance descriptions, neither tide-removal approach yielded a model-robust apparent vertical-rate field. The campaign resolved spatial patterns of horizontal motion and vertical tidal response, while covariance testing identified the limits of apparent vertical-rate inference from short GNSS records.

title: Warming Trends on the Hurd Peninsula of Livingston Island, Antarctica, Between 2000 and 2024, and Improvements in the Estimation of Air Temperature Using C6.1 MODIS LST Data
abstract: Analysing the spatial and temporal variability of near-surface air temperature (Ta) is essential for assessing climate change, particularly in polar regions such as the maritime Antarctic, where observational studies remain comparatively scarce. In areas with sparse meteorological networks, satellite observations provide a valuable means of extending station-based analyses and generating spatially distributed Ta maps. This study analyses updated Ta records from six meteorological stations on the Hurd Peninsula, Livingston Island, for 2000–2024, with particular attention to temperature changes since 2016, and evaluates Ta estimation models based on MODIS Terra daytime LST Collection 6.1 data. The analysis of the Ta time series showed significant warming over the complete 2000–2024 period, with trends ranging from 0.53 to 1.27 °C decade−1, and a clear shift towards warming after 2016. While the 2000–2015 period showed spatially contrasting trends, including cooling at JCI, positive trends were observed at all analysed stations during 2016–2024, ranging from 0.40 to 1.33 °C decade−1 and highlighting substantial local variability across the Hurd Peninsula. The global Ta model, developed using data from all six stations and based on MODIS Terra daytime LST and spatiotemporal variables, achieved a performance comparable to that obtained with Collection 6, with R2 = 0.77 and a cross-validated RMSE of 2.23 °C. The results also showed that rigorous filtering of the MODIS LST observations is essential: retaining only good-quality data and excluding observations with |view angle| > 45° substantially reduced dispersion in the Ta–LST relationship and removed unrealistically low LST values. The introduction of this view-angle threshold represents a new filtering step with respect to our previous studies.

title: Modelling the effects of proglacial lake filling and drainage on lake-terminating glacier dynamics
abstract: Ice sheet/glacier retreat is driving expansion of glacial lakes impounded at the ice margin. Using an ice sheet model, we find that lake filling and drainage causes systematic changes to glacier thickness, velocity and mass loss. Rising lake levels dramatically increase mass loss as the ice margin becomes buoyant, while rapid lake drainage can drive crevassing and destabilise the margin. Steady lake drainage, in contrast, has a stabilising effect, and may mitigate mass loss and flood hazards.

title: Milanković’s Theory of Ice Ages and Serbian Loess
abstract: The text deals with Milanković’s Mathematical–Astronomical Theory of Ice Ages and its connection with Serbian loess. Here it is recalled, put into the context of the people who collaborated with Milanković during his work (W. Köppen, A. Wegener, V. Mišković, W. Jardetzky, D. Mitrinović, and S. Fempl), and it points to its 50th anniversary of verification in the journal Science. Then, the Theory is compared with magnetic susceptibility (MS) profiles of two Serbian loess–paleosol sequences (Mošorin and Stari Slankamen) by (i) showing side-by-side the Milanković’s Insolation Curves and the MS Curves over the last 600,000 years and (ii) discussing the relation of the MS spectral components and the orbital (eccentricity, obliquity, and precession) and terrestrial (solar constant and albedo) forcing of Milankovic’sTheory. In addition to the similarities between Milanković’s Insolation Curves and the MS Curves, there are discrepancies, the causes of which are analyzed in detail. The text ends with a biographical section on Milanković’s voyages down the Danube and the StariSlankamen profile, where in the layers of loess there are visual traces of the change in glacial (Ice Ages), cold intervals and interglacial (Inter Ice Ages), warm intervals in the geological history of the Earth. These traces match relatively well with Milanković’s Insolation Curves, which he could not have known during his many passes. In the conclusion, suggestions are given on how to reduce the discrepancies between Milanković’s Insolation Curves and the MS Curves and thereby improve paleoclimatological research.

title: Disentangling positional change from intensity in the palaeoclimate reconstruction of circulation patterns
abstract: Abstract Under ongoing anthropogenic climate change, the impacts of forcing on climate circulation patterns, such as ocean currents and wind belts, are an area of particular scientific interest. Due to the complexity of the system, these subsystem patterns can exhibit multi-dimensional variability such as strength change or feature migration. However, conventional proxy-based reconstructions risk conflating positional shifts with intensity changes, thereby obscuring the true mode of past variability and potentially impeding the accuracy of hindcasts and predictions. Here, we present this issue and discuss three subsystems where previous work has attempted to disentangle spatial and magnitudinal change, namely the Gulf Stream, Intertropical Convergence Zone, and Southern Hemisphere westerly winds. Our analysis of deployed methodologies finds that studies principally employ spatial networks and dimension-specific proxies to separate these compounding effects. We emphasise the importance of incorporating this interpretation challenge into future study design and highlight the need for new disentanglement methods. This review synthesises existing disentanglement approaches, provides a concise conceptual framing, and offers practical recommendations for study design.

title: Tracking danger on the peaks
abstract: The Earth is warming, but not all regions are warming equally. In high mountain areas, temperatures are generally increasing by 1.5 to 2 times the global average, sometimes with devastating consequences. A small or gradual change in the mountain cryosphere—perhaps progressive thawing of frozen ground or a flood from a small glacial lake—can suddenly turn into a cascade of catastrophes with enormous ramifications. Monitoring systems for the cryosphere in high mountain areas have traditionally been designed to look at individual components and changes. What are the temperature and depth of the permafrost, or how much area is covered by snow, and what is the related avalanche danger? Many of the monitoring and warning systems were designed for historical patterns of snowfall or rainfall, and a river gauge may no longer be adequate if there is greater flow in the rainy season, or increased sediment that could damage the gauge.

title: Ground-Penetrating Radar Ice-Thickness Survey and 3D Bed-Topography Modelling of the Weigele Glacier Constrained by Borehole-Calibrated Radar Velocity
abstract: Glacier thickness and subglacial bed topography are fundamental parameters for ice-volume estimation of mountain glaciers; in regions where direct field observations are sparse, these parameters remain weakly constrained in space. This study deployed a closed-loop ground-penetrating radar (GPR) survey network on Weigele Glacier in the Animaqing Mountains and calibrated the radar wave velocity using a GPR profile that crossed an in situ borehole. The borehole-calibrated effective radar wave velocity is 0.17018 m·ns−1, which is 1.30% higher than the commonly used default value of 0.168 m·ns−1. Based on 1477 GPR ice-thickness measurements and zero-thickness boundary points at the upper glacier margin, Gaussian process regression was used to interpolate ice thickness on a 5 m horizontal grid. Leave-one-profile-out cross-validation showed that adding the ice-surface slope covariate changed the model error only slightly (RMSE of 85.48 m) relative to the coordinate-only baseline model (RMSE of 85.44 m); the final reconstruction therefore adopted horizontal coordinates as predictors. Within the 0.481 km2 GPR modelling domain, the maximum measured ice thickness is 258.328 m, the mean interpolated ice thickness is 130.10 m, and the ice volume is 0.06260 km3. The reconstructed bed exhibits a pronounced longitudinal trough, and the low-lying bed corresponds spatially to the main thick-ice zone. Boundary-condition sensitivity tests yield an ice-volume range of 0.04767–0.07531 km3. These volume estimates correspond to the modelling domain covered by the GPR network.

title: Historical Multidecadal Variability of Intraseasonal Features of Sahel Rainfall in CMIP6 Models and Observations
abstract: Abstract We compare observations with seven large ensembles of CMIP6 historical simulations to understand the role that external forcings and internal variability may have played in modulating the frequency and intensity of daily rainfall, and the duration of the rainy season in the Sahel. We compare three periods: [1950–1970], [1970–1990] and [1994–2014]. The results show that the anomalously wet [1950–1970] and [1994–2014] periods are characterized by more extreme rainfall days and longer monsoon seasons than the drier [1970–1990] period. In exploring the contributions of anthropogenic aerosols (AAs) and greenhouse gases (GHGs) in both transitions, we find results to be consistent with partial cancellation of the effects of AA and GHG in the [1950–1970] to [1970–1990] transition to drought, which allows internal variability to contribute significantly, and with the emergence of the external forcing effect in the [1970–1990] to [1994–2014] recovery. In particular, the shift of AA emissions from North America and Europe to Asia between [1970–1990] and [1994–2014] increases the number of extreme rainy days and lengthens the wet season. The increase in GHG concentrations between these two periods also acts to increase the number of extreme rainy days. However, this effect is not statistically significant in all models. Finally, in all the models analyzed, we cannot discard the fact that the individual effects of AAs and GHGs add up linearly in setting the total precipitation change.

title: A new high-resolution daily mean South China Sea Ocean Reanalysis dataset: SCSORA
abstract: This research presents a high-resolution ocean reanalysis dataset for the South China Sea covering 2001 to 2024. The dataset assimilates satellite remote sensing data and in-situ observations. It provides daily mean three-dimensional fields of temperature, salinity, currents, and sea surface height. Validation results show good agreement with observations. The dataset has been used to support studies of marine heatwaves, mesoscale eddies, and related processes in this important region.

title: Comparing Data-Driven and Numerical Weather Prediction Forecasts of Extreme Weather: A Review
abstract: arXiv:2611.23863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data-driven weather forecasting models, chiefly trained on reanalysis data, now match or beat physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) models on most headline scores, but whether this advantage extends to extreme weather is contested. We review peer-reviewed studies that directly compare data-driven forecasts with NWP for extremes, from nowcasting to subseasonal lead times. We discuss grey literature in the outlook but do not include it in the formal review. There is good agreement on the fact that data-driven models mostly outperform NWP on temperature extremes, tropical cyclone tracks and the location of synoptic features across time scales. The evidence is mixed for extreme precipitation and feature-based extreme event detection such as extremes related to atmospheric rivers, while it leans toward better NWP performance for estimating event intensity. For record-breaking events that lie outside the training distribution, the evidence is narrower. Nonetheless, both a systematic global evaluation and several case studies find that physics-based models retain the advantage, with data-driven models underestimating both the frequency and the magnitude of records. Hybrid systems that post-process NWP with machine-learning (ML), or couple data-driven forecasts with physics-based models, deliver some of the largest and most consistent gains. We argue that headline scores, verification choices and case selection explain much of the apparent disagreement in the literature, and provide recommendations for a more trustworthy and interpretable evaluation of data-driven models for extreme and record-breaking weather.

title: How abruptly did the Holocene Green Sahara end?
abstract: To move the long-standing debate of whether the vegetation changes in the Sahara during the last 8000 years occurred abruptly or gradually we propose a new quantitative metric. Our analysis of model and proxy data suggests the vegetation composition in the Holocene Sahara can undergo substantially more abrupt transitions than total vegetation cover, and a gradual expansion of the Sahara can be accompanied by abrupt, step-like transitions within local ecosystems.

title: Run it Back: Autoregression vs. Video Diffusion for Final-Conditioned Weather Trajectories
abstract: arXiv:2611.21521v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Low-likelihood, high-impact extremes are projected to increase in severity and frequency in a warming climate. Sampling the precursors that lead to these events traditionally requires massive ensembles that scale poorly with lead time and rarity, and typical rare-event sampling and ensemble-boosting methods do not show how a single extreme might arise from diverse synoptic precursors. Recently, Lin et al.\ (2026) showed this is possible with final-conditioned 66-hour trajectories (trajectories constrained to end at an observed state) from cBottle-video, a pre-trained, off-the-shelf video diffusion climate emulator not explicitly fine-tuned for this task (Brenowitz et al., 2025). However, its ensembles were underdispersed and geostrophically inconsistent, and it reproduces conditioned frames only approximately, hindering autoregressive rollout. Here, we train Rewind-AR, a backward-in-time probabilistic autoregressive model with a FourCastNet~3 backbone (Bonev et al., 2025), and generate final-conditioned ensembles for the same three cases: the 2021 Pacific Northwest heatwave, Hurricane Ian, and Superstorm Sandy (in the Supplementary Information). The leading modes of Rewind-AR's antecedent 500 hPa geopotential height explain far more of the across-member variance than cBottle-video's for both hurricane position and heatwave surface temperature, and Rewind-AR better reproduces the day-over-day heatwave intensification observed in ERA5. Finally, geostrophic inconsistencies close to the conditioning frame seen in cBottle-video are not reproduced by Rewind-AR. Nevertheless, up to 22\% of Rewind-AR members become numerically unstable within 66 hours, so improving rollout physical consistency and stability over long lead times is a natural next step.

abstract: The land surface shapes our weather and climate by controlling how heat and water move between the ground and the air, so the models representing it matter enormously. title: Importance of glacier shrinkage for sustaining runoff in Panj River of Pamir, Central Asia
abstract: Study region The study area is the Panj River basin, situated in the upper reaches of the Amu Darya basin. Study focus Glacier and snowmelt runoff are vital for sustaining streamflow in the Panj River Basin, a key cryospheric water source region in Central Asia. However, the impacts of glacier retreat, snow changes, and precipitation variability on long-term runoff remain unclear under global warming. This study applied the Hydrologiska Byråns Vattenbalansavdelning (HBV) model to quantify runoff components, including rainfall, snowmelt, and glacier runoff, and integrated the Budyko framework, scenario simulations, and glacier retreat experiments to assess runoff drivers and the hydrological response to glacier loss. New hydrological insights The results showed that total runoff, rainfall runoff, and snowmelt runoff exhibited significant decreasing trends during 1982–2020, whereas glacier runoff increased, reflecting a temporary compensation effect from enhanced glacier melt under climate warming. Meltwater runoff accounted for 67.9% of total runoff and played an important role in regulating streamflow, particularly during dry years. Attribution analysis revealed that runoff changes were mainly controlled by climatic factors (122.5%), with precipitation being the dominant driver, while human activities (−22.5%) partially offset the decline in runoff. Glacier retreat scenarios indicated that continued glacier loss would reduce summer meltwater supply and may alter the seasonal distribution of runoff, with potential implications for the stability of downstream water supply. The impacts of glacier change on mountain runoff processes and regional water resources provide a basis for understanding potential changes in downstream water availability in Central Asia.

title: WeatherDreamer: Learning a World Model from Multimodal Earth Observations
abstract: arXiv:2611.18393v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine learning weather models now rival operational global forecasts but still start from analyses produced by separate, expensive data assimilation (DA) systems, which for global models are typically updated every six hours. Observation-to-observation models avoid this dependence, but most omit the recursive filtering cycle that lets DA systems carry a background state through sparse, irregular observations. We introduce WeatherDreamer, a world model that learns this cycle end-to-end from 18 global observing systems, without reanalysis. It infers a latent state from observations, carries it forward hour by hour with learned dynamics, corrects it each hour with new observations, and can predict what any of its observing systems would measure at any location. At held-out stations, its ensembles beat NOAA's Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) for temperature, dew point and wind out to 12 h and are better calibrated than GEFS and the ECMWF ensemble. Precipitation, cloud-top height and solar irradiance, never inputs at inference, are inferred with skill matching or exceeding operational products at short leads. Against the first guess of NOAA's Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) DA system, WeatherDreamer's short-range departures are within 10% of GSI's at surface stations and within 25% for moisture-sensitive microwave channels, but up to five times larger for temperature-sounding channels. Never given observation errors, its learned update assumes errors close to known instrument and retrieval errors of microwave sounders and scatterometer winds. WeatherDreamer also separates viewing geometry from atmospheric state, recovering 83-96% of observed limb darkening and producing seamless nadir-view imagery. Producing an hourly global analysis in about 1.5 minutes on one GPU, WeatherDreamer shows that assimilation and forecasting can be learned together directly from observations.

title: Uncertainty Estimate for Extended Reconstructed Sea Surface Temperature Version 6 (ERSSTv6)
abstract: Abstract The NOAA Extended Reconstructed Sea Surface Temperature version 6 (ERSSTv6) provides a globally complete monthly SST dataset from 1850 to present, reconstructed from ship, buoy, and near-surface Argo observations using an artificial neural network (ANN) approach. ERSSTv6 incorporates enhanced quality control, large-scale spatial filtering, and an updated ice–SST proxy and includes an operationally feasible and physically consistent uncertainty framework that supports robust assessments of SST variability, trends, and ocean-related applications. We quantify total SST uncertainty as the combination of parametric and reconstruction uncertainties. Parametric uncertainty is estimated from a 1000-member ensemble generated by perturbing 30 internal parameters, including ANN coefficients, quality control, bias adjustments, and ice-SST proxy. ANN-related uncertainty is approximated using a random perturbation (RP) to ANN coefficients, whose magnitude is calibrated by validation errors. Reconstruction uncertainty is assessed with a 500-member ensemble applied to a space-time-complete reference dataset, representing algorithmic error under ideal observations. Results show that grid-scale uncertainty is largest in regions with strong SST variability and sparse data, including western boundary currents, the eastern equatorial Pacific, and ice-covered areas, with global mean uncertainty decreasing from 0.4°–0.5°C in the 1850s to ∼0.3°C after 1950. Uncertainty in global mean SST is smaller, ranging from 0.06°–0.08°C in the 1850s to ∼0.02°C in recent decades. Factor analysis indicates that ANN RP dominates the grid-scale uncertainty, while ship bias correction and ice–SST proxy dominate the uncertainty of global-mean SST. Comparisons show that both SST and its uncertainty in ERSSTv6 are broadly consistent with those other SST products.

title: Climate and glacier geometry dominate global glacier–lake interactions
abstract: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02808-5 The contribution of glacial lakes to glacier mass loss is unclear. abstract: Sub-annual glacier surface velocity derived from remote sensing images are receiving increasing attention. title: Discrepancies and Consistencies in Multi-Source Estimates of Eurasian Spring Snowmelt During 1982–2014
abstract: Snow alters land–atmosphere energy and moisture exchanges via albedo and hydrological effects, markedly impacting subseasonal-to-seasonal climate variability. While Earth observations and model-based products form the foundation for investigating snow–climate interactions, comprehensive assessments of snowmelt, which directly reflects snow-induced hydrological and thermal anomalies, remain scarce compared to those of conventional snow mass variables. Benchmarked against the satellite–in situ blended GlobSnow data, this study comprehensively evaluates the discrepancies and consistencies of Eurasian spring snowmelt (spring snow water equivalent difference, SSD) across six multi-source datasets (SnowCCI, JRA-3Q, ERA5-Land, MERRA-2, GLDAS-NOAH, and FLDAS) during 1982–2014. The results reveal that satellite-based SnowCCI and JRA-3Q exhibit the highest consistency with GlobSnow in reproducing the spatial distribution, temporal variability, and dominant east–west dipole mode of Eurasian SSD. Specifically, they accurately capture its clear latitudinal zonation and a distinct dipole-like trend, characterized by decreasing SSD over western Eurasia and increasing SSD over eastern Eurasia. Conversely, ERA5-Land and MERRA-2 reasonably capture the temporal evolution of SSD but tend to overestimate variability amplitudes. GLDAS-NOAH exhibits relatively weak regional heterogeneity and underestimates SSD variability, whereas FLDAS tends to overestimate variability amplitudes and shows pronounced regional dependence. Further analysis suggests that uncertainties in snowfall simulations may be a major source of discrepancies in SSD estimation, although their relative contribution remains uncertain. These findings provide crucial insights for selecting appropriate datasets in snow–climate research and underscore the importance of dataset uncertainty quantification in subseasonal-to-seasonal climate prediction.

title: Tracing Uncertainties of Extreme El Ni\~{n}o Prediction to Mesoscale Ocean Currents
abstract: arXiv:2611.17854v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The predictability of the El Ni\~{n}o-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) has historically been linked to large-scale errors in models' initial conditions such as heat content and surface wind stress. Here we demonstrate that these slowly evolving errors may ultimately originate from mesoscale errors in initial oceanic states that are common in current models and ocean observation systems. This hidden source of ENSO forecast uncertainty, in terms of mesoscale ocean-current errors, is convincingly exposed by the conditional nonlinear optimal perturbation (CNOP) method applied to a differentiable ocean AI model. The CNOP-identified most influential current errors are strongly event-dependent. For the 1997/98 El Ni\~{n}o, the initial current errors in the eastern Pacific results in the largest forecast error through locally suppressing original subsurface warming. For the 2015/16 event, the dominate error originates from the western Pacific, which reorganizes upper ocean temperature structure and affects the eastern Pacific through the equatorial waveguide. Further analysis reveals that these current errors perturb mesoscale eddy count and eddy kinetic energy triggering large-scale temperature errors that hinder El Ni\~{n}o development. The timing of the maximum growth rate of the obtained CNOP error is well aligned with the spring predictability barrier of ENSO, and the error structures are reflected in simulated analysis errors caused by unresolved mesoscale currents. These findings extend the potential source of ENSO predictability beyond large-scale thermal signals, reveal for the first time an uncharted route of ENSO forecast failure, and provide an important physical basis for targeted ocean observations and data assimilation in the future.

title: The ocean–atmosphere turbulent flux algorithm in E3SMv2 does not always converge to unique and physical solutions:  analysis and potential remedy
abstract: Accurately computing ocean–atmosphere turbulent fluxes, which measure the transfer of momentum, heat, and water between the Earth and its oceans, in Earth system models is important for overall model accuracy. Under certain meteorological conditions, the set of equations utilized in many Earth system models to parameterize these fluxes can have no solution or more than one solution. Modifying the equations to address these issues leads to substantial changes to the simulated turbulent fluxes.

title: Learning Calibrated and Samplable Predictive Distributions of Surface-Ocean $\Delta p$CO$_2$ Using Tabular Diffusion Models
abstract: arXiv:2611.21769v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The ocean absorbs almost 30% of anthropogenic CO$_2$ emissions, but quantifying this sink requires estimating surface-ocean CO$_2$ from observations that are sparse in space and time. Most existing machine-learning estimates of this field are deterministic, giving a single value per grid point, with uncertainty approximated post hoc via residuals, ensembles, or prescribed distributions. We instead learn a conditional predictive distribution for each observation: using Treeffuser, a conditional diffusion model with gradient-boosted-tree score functions, we estimate the full predictive distribution of $\Delta p$CO$_2$ (the sea-air $p$CO$_2$ difference) from 13 environmental, spatial, and temporal predictors. On a held-out SOCAT test set, Treeffuser attains the lowest continuous ranked probability score among the uncertainty-quantification methods evaluated (8.229 $\mu$atm) and the coverage closest to the nominal 68% / 95% levels (0.686 / 0.930), while retaining point-prediction skill comparable to a deterministic XGBoost baseline (RMSE 18.4 vs. 17.7 $\mu$atm; $R^2$ 0.77 vs. 0.79). These results show that conditional diffusion can provide well-calibrated, observation-level uncertainties while largely preserving point-prediction skill. Because Treeffuser is generative, its samples can support probabilistic analyses of $\Delta p$CO$_2$; extending this to spatially coherent field reconstruction will require modeling dependence across grid cells and evaluation on spatially held-out data.

title: A regime dependent parameterization of the refractive-index structure parameter $C_n^2$
abstract: arXiv:2611.22641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vertical profiles of the refractive-index (RI) structure parameter, $C_n^2$, are required in atmospheric-optics calculations. The Hufnagel--Valley (HV) model is a useful reference profile and it is widely used however, it is difficult to say that it produces consistent results at the observed altitude, magnitude, and thickness of all turbulent layers and it can diverge from realistic measurements in particular height ranges, sites, and stability regimes. This study develops a regime-dependent RI structure parameter considering meteorological conditions and, more importantly, it provides a structure that can be calibrated against measured $C_n^2$ throughout the surface layer (SL), atmospheric boundary layer (ABL), and free atmosphere. The formulation combines SL including distinct unstable, near-neutral, and stable limits; convective ABL; and free-atmospheric turbulence when kinetic-energy and temperature-variance dissipation rates are available. The $C_n^2$ is formed by weighting the contribution of different layers. We use representative, physically plausible meteorological profiles to examine the model's limiting behavior, transitions between atmospheric regimes, continuity, sensitivity to its parameters, and propagation-related differences from the HV 5/7 model. The intended outcome is a measurement-calibrated model that remains physically interpretable across meteorological regimes.

Evaluation of machine-learning and deep-learning SPEI drought forecasts against persistence across timescales and lead times in Bangladesh
abstract: arXiv:2611.25075v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bangladesh, home to nearly 178 million people, is highly vulnerable to recurring droughts that threaten food security and rural livelihoods. Machine-learning and deep-learning models are increasingly used to forecast drought indices such as the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI). Most studies report accuracy without a persistence reference, although accumulated indices are strongly autocorrelated, and seldom test drought detection, longer leads or variation between training runs. This study forecast SPEI at 3-, 6- and 12-month timescales one to three months ahead for the eight divisions of Bangladesh, using ERA5 reanalysis checked against 35 Bangladesh Meteorological Department stations. Five models, XGBoost, CNN, Bi-LSTM, CNN-BiLSTM and CEEMDAN-BiLSTM, were trained with five seeds each, scored on accuracy, skill against persistence and drought detection, and interpreted with Shapley values. At a one-month lead, the CNN-BiLSTM and Bi-LSTM beat persistence clearly at SPEI-3 and SPEI-6 (skill 0.408 and 0.350), while at SPEI-12 a Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.872 barely exceeded persistence (0.850). Skill and detection could disagree: at SPEI-3 and a three-month lead, XGBoost had the highest skill (0.439) yet detected none of the 119 drought months. Only at SPEI-6 did the forecasts beat persistence significantly and match its detection at all three leads, with fewer false alarms. At SPEI-12, gains were small or absent and varied between seeds. The forecasts kept 76-80% of their correlation against station-derived SPEI and relied mainly on precipitation and lagged SPEI. Forecasts should therefore be judged on skill against persistence and detection across several seeds, not on accuracy alone. In Bangladesh, SPEI-6 forecasts can support early warning up to three months ahead and SPEI-3 forecasts one month ahead, while SPEI-12 is better suited to monitoring.

title: Reef resilience and demise on the NW shelf of Australia during the warm Miocene
abstract: Abstract During the Miocene, sea surface temperature (SSTs) and CO 2 exceeded modern levels. Given the current decline of coral reefs due to rising summer temperatures, it is unclear how extensive reef systems developed and thrived in a warm Miocene world. This problem is exacerbated by a lack of SST reconstructions. Here, we use TEX 86 H to reconstruct summer SSTs between 5.0 and 17.4 Ma from a sediment core (IODP Site U1464) within the Miocene NW Australian shelf Barrier Reef system. During the Miocene Climate Optimum, summer SSTs reached up to 34 °C. However, stable arid conditions and low subsidence rates allowed the reef to expand. Around 6 Ma, SSTs were ideal for coral reef growth, but increased terrestrial input and subsidence caused the relatively rapid collapse of almost all reefs. Multiple environmental stressors culminated in reef drowning. Therefore, a barrier reef system formed at > 30 °C SSTs, but this was only possible under otherwise ideal conditions.
